1	# Task 13: Coral reef underwater with camera orbit
2	
3	Build a single-page browser app with the provided framework, served by vite. It must render one full-viewport canvas with id #app. The scene is a shallow tropical coral reef seen underwater. Show a sandy seabed with rippled patterns, several coral formations in different shapes (branching, rounded brain, fan or tube shapes) and colours, and swaying seaweed or anemones. A school of at least 30 small fish should swim in a loose group, plus 2 or more larger solitary fish on their own paths. Sunlight should enter from above, with a bluish-green water tint, depth-based colour fade, and drifting caustic-like light patterns on the sand. A few bubbles or particles should rise slowly. The camera orbits slowly around the reef centre at a gentle height, with a slight bob, and no user input is needed. Do not rely on external downloads; build everything from simple procedural shapes.

I'm uncertain about the handle approach since docs are thin, so I'll go with the safer documented pattern using runtime nodes with setPosition for animation. Planning node counts now: fish groups, bubbles as individual spheres, and seaweed elements.

Actually, nested-group seaweed with per-frame rotation calls adds too many nodes and updates, so I'm leaning toward a GPU-based approach instead: merge the seaweed blades into one static mesh and use a vertex shader to displace them based on height and time, matching the shader technique I'm already using for the sand, which should be both more efficient and visually smoother.

I'm encoding height along the blade and a phase/color selector into the uv coordinates, then using those to drive both displacement and coloring in the shader -- displacing more near the tip with a sine wave offset by phase, and coloring with a gradient that shifts between dark green, olive, and pink depending on uv.y. This same sway shader can be reused for anemone tentacles too, just swapping the color palette, so I can share one material across different swaying vegetation types.

I'll drive the sway with a time uniform passed through as a varying, set up as a mutable runtime node similar to the water setup. For underwater fog, I'm writing a shared GLSL function that fades color toward the fog color based on camera distance and darkens things further down the water column, and I need the standard PBR fog settings to roughly match this custom falloff so the whole scene reads consistently.

Since colors converge to the fog color at distance anyway, I'll pick a density around 0.045 for the shader's exponential falloff, accepting minor mismatch with the engine's own exp² fog on regular objects. For the background, instead of a flat solid color I'm leaning toward a sky gradient where the zenith is lighter (suggesting sunlit water near the surface) and the horizon matches the fog color, so looking around underwater feels cohesive rather than hitting a flat void.

Now I'm working through the geometry: with the camera low and tilted slightly down, I need the seabed plane large enough and the fog density tuned so the sand's edge fades out before it's visible rather than creating a hard cutoff. I'm testing density values like 0.06 against seabed sizes like 80×80 to make sure the edge sits far enough past the point where fog has reduced visibility to a small fraction, while still keeping ripple detail resolved near the camera.

I'm also layering an extra distance-based fade in the custom shader to guarantee a full fog-color blend by around 34 units out, and reconsidering mesh resolution tradeoffs -- balancing vertex count against ripple wavelength, and deciding to push fine ripple detail into the fragment shader's normal calculation rather than relying solely on mesh geometry.

Now I'm tightening the seabed bounds to ±30 units with 0.3m cells, and working out the fog falloff math given the camera sits at roughly 11 units from center -- edge points range from 19 to 41 units away, so I'm tuning a smoothstep fog threshold around 22-32 to make sure reef objects stay visible while distant terrain fades cleanly into fog at the edges.

Now I'm blending the edge fade into a radial falloff based on distance from center, then shifting focus to the sand shader's warm coloring under blue-green filtered sunlight, and sketching out a caustics function using layered sine-warped cellular noise.

I'm thinking through a hue-and-value encoding scheme using UV coordinates to drive an HSV-to-RGB palette lookup, fixing saturation to keep things pastel while varying hue and brightness per coral type, and deciding whether this added complexity is worth the payoff for a cohesive caustic-lit underwater look.

One shared reef shader seems the way to go, combining directional/hemisphere lighting with caustics masked by upward normals and height fade, plus fog, applied across seabed, corals, rocks, and swaying seaweed, while fish stick to standard PBR with fog for consistency. I'm also weighing a cheap fake AO trick that darkens coral bases near the terrain using height-based vertex data.

For the sway variation, I'm planning to generate two shader variants from one JS function using a boolean flag rather than relying on uncertain `defines` injection, each getting its own clock uniform updated per frame, with UV channels repurposed to encode hue and value data.

Writing the HSV-to-RGB conversion function...

Now I'm thinking about how to encode saturation variation alongside hue in a single UV coordinate, since each colony vertex needs its own color but variation within a surface should still interpolate smoothly.

Writing mesh builder class...

For outward-facing normals I'll flip based on direction from a center point when needed, but for closed meshes consistent winding should avoid ever seeing backfaces, so I'll set materials to double-sided and rely on correct vertex normals rather than fragment shader tricks.

For tubes, I'm now working out the geometry: computing frames along a path via parallel transport, with tangents from neighboring points and rotation-minimizing normal updates to avoid twisting, then building ring vertices around each path point.

For the open top of a tube sponge, I'll add a dark inner disc capping the rim, giving the illusion of depth without fully modeling an inner wall — just a fan of triangles with low value facing upward. Then I'll move to colony generators, starting with recursive branching logic for staghorn coral.

Each branch curves upward through a few points with tapering radius, spawning 2-3 children at the end with randomized upward-biased direction, going 3-4 levels deep. I'm budgeting the triangle count per colony: roughly 40 branches total across depth levels, each costing about 36 triangles, landing near 1.4k triangles for three differently colored colonies (orange, pink, purple/blue) — well within budget.

Now I'm sketching brain coral as a dome shape, defining its surface using a polar/azimuthal parameterization with slight radius variation to give it that wrinkled, folded look.

For the brain coral's surface texture, I'm designing a labyrinth-like groove pattern using layered sine functions to create cell-like ridges, then picking a fine enough grid (96×48) to resolve the groove wavelength properly, with the dome embedded partway into the ground. Next I'm moving on to a fan coral shape — an upright flattened fan where width grows with height and a gentle sine wave gives it some depth undulation.

For colouring, instead of trying to cut alpha holes for a lattice look, I'll just use vein-like colour modulation across the surface. Then I'm reconsidering the structure entirely — building the fan coral as a gorgonian-style lattice of thin tubes, with radial spokes fanning out from a base point and cross-links between them for a webbed look.

Now I'm planning out the remaining coral types: tube/organ-pipe coral clusters with tapered tubes and dark opening discs in yellow/orange/purple; table coral as a rippled disc on a stalk in teal; lumpy greyish rocks underneath; and seaweed blades built as ribbon strips that sway.

For the seaweed shader, I'm working out blade geometry tapering in width toward the tip, with grass-like heights around 0.8-1.8m for a shallow reef setting, green hues with olive variation, and a sway function that bends each blade based on height-squared and a position-based phase offset so they don't move in unison.

I'm separating amplitude by material type since tall seaweed needs more sway (0.35) while short anemone tentacles need much less (0.06) to avoid unrealistic swinging, meaning each gets its own shader instance with a distinct amplitude uniform.

For anemones specifically, I'm building each one from a static base column plus ~40 thin tentacle tubes radiating from a ring, each tentacle being a few segments of low-poly tube geometry, keeping the column's height parameter at zero so it stays rigid while only the tentacles sway.

For the shader, I'm writing fragment lighting logic that flips the normal based on face orientation, computes diffuse lighting from a sun direction angled from above, and blends in a sky-tinted ambient term based on the upward-facing component of the normal.

I'm also layering in a caustics effect, projecting sun-driven light patterns onto surfaces scaled by depth and the vertical component of the normal, mimicking how real underwater caustics appear on sunlit surfaces.

I'm uncertain whether the shader's output color is treated as linear or sRGB by the renderer, which could create a slight mismatch between my fog constants and the built-in scene fog. I'll accept the approximation and just make sure standard objects rely on the scene's native fog while only the fish shader uses my custom fog math.

Now I'm designing the fish school of 36, building each as a group with a body sphere and oriented tail cone, working out non-uniform scaling so each fish gets an elongated, flattened body shape.

For orientation, I'm keeping it simple: each fish's forward axis is +x locally, rotated only about Y by its yaw angle derived from atan2 of its velocity components, skipping pitch to avoid Euler-order ambiguity.

Rather than animating a separate tail joint, I'll fake the swimming wiggle cheaply by jittering the whole fish's yaw with a sine wave over time plus a phase offset per fish. For the body itself, I'm pairing an ellipsoid body with a flattened cone for the tail, rotated about Z so its apex meets the body and its wide base trails behind.

Still building the fin geometry rotation. For coloring the school, I'm thinking golden yellow (#ffc830) as the dominant body color across most of the 36 fish, maybe with a handful in a contrasting silver-blue to break up the uniformity.

I'll settle on 28 gold fish and 8 coral-orange ones for subtle variation. For the three large solitary fish, I'm planning distinct species built from primitives (body, tail fin, dorsal fin, eye): a tall bluish-yellow angelfish disc, a brown-red grouper, and a silvery barracuda, each moving along its own ellipse or Lissajous path with different radius, height, and speed within the reef bounds. The small school will follow a loose group behavior -- a center path with individual offset wobble that slowly drifts.

Writing path equations...

Checking that the camera's vertical field of view works geometrically with the orbit radius, and keeping corals within a tighter inner ring so the fish school's wider path stays clear of them, swimming a bit higher above the reef.

Setting the school's elliptical path dimensions and angular speed so the fish move at a natural 1.2 m/s, and driving the caustic shader animation off a scaled clock time. I'm weighing whether to add visible light shafts for the sunlight, since the brief calls for a bluish-green depth fade and caustic patterns but doesn't explicitly require god rays, and I want to avoid faking glows with flat emissive cards.

Checking whether the water surface would even be visible from the camera's position and pitch — it mostly won't be, so I'll skip rendering a surface plane and instead rely on a gradient sky plus a directional light from above tinted bluish-green to sell the sunlight effect, skipping risky shaft or volumetric fog effects. For post-processing I'll keep things light, maybe just a subtle vignette, and skip bloom.

I'm also weighing whether to start from a preset look or build the underwater palette manually, so I should check the looks list for something like "underwater" before deciding.
